subtopic: Little's Law / ILP + MLP requirements for latency hiding
learningObjective: Apply Little's Law at the instruction/memory level to reason about the concurrency required to fully hide arithmetic and memory latency.
profileData: Kernel X (memory-bound, single outstanding load per warp): occupancy 100%, HBM throughput 40% of peak. Kernel Y (memory-bound, 8 outstanding loads per warp): occupancy 25%, HBM throughput 90% of peak. Both target A100, N=32M elements.
stem: Consider a memory-bound GPU kernel. Which of the following statements correctly apply Little's Law to reasoning about latency hiding? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: To fully hide DRAM latency, the SM must maintain enough outstanding memory requests such that Little's Law (concurrency = bandwidth × latency) is satisfied; this is why kernels need many warps and each warp needs multiple outstanding loads.

Low occupancy can still saturate HBM if each active warp issues many in-flight loads simultaneously (high memory-level parallelism per warp), because Little's Law counts total outstanding requests, not warp count.
Once occupancy reaches 100%, latency hiding is guaranteed regardless of per-thread memory-level parallelism.

For compute latency (arithmetic pipeline), Little's Law analogously requires enough independent instructions in flight per warp scheduler; ILP within a warp complements TLP across warps to hide compute-pipeline latency.

explanation: A: This is the standard application of Little's Law to memory-level parallelism (MLP) on GPUs. B: Volkov and others show that low-occupancy kernels can saturate HBM if each warp has enough outstanding loads; occupancy is one way to achieve concurrency, not the only way. C is wrong: 100% occupancy without per-warp MLP still cannot saturate DRAM if each warp issues at most one outstanding load. D: ILP hides arithmetic pipeline latency analogously — a compute pipeline with L cycles of latency needs L independent instructions in flight to be fully utilized.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: Little's Law for MLP; total outstanding requests = BW × latency.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: low-occupancy high-MLP kernels can saturate memory (Volkov's classic result).
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: occupancy alone does not guarantee latency hiding; per-warp MLP matters.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: ILP + TLP combine to hide compute-pipeline latency.

assumptions: Kernel is bandwidth or latency limited on either memory or arithmetic pipelines.
Warp scheduler can issue independent instructions from a warp when ready.
nonImplications: Does not imply low-occupancy kernels are always fine; when per-warp MLP is limited (e.g., data-dependent loads), occupancy is the fallback.
Does not imply that any technique alone (ILP, TLP, MLP) suffices; realistic kernels mix all three.

distractorRationales.C: Overgeneralizes occupancy as a sufficient condition for latency hiding.

sourceRefs.locator: Latency hiding via MLP and occupancy

performanceClaim.scope: GPU latency hiding via combined MLP/ILP/TLP; Little's Law application
